To coast means to move forward or make progress without putting in any real effort — because something else is doing the work for you. That something could be gravity, momentum, or a past advantage you built up earlier.

A simple image to anchor this: imagine you are on a bicycle, going downhill, and you lift your feet off the pedals. You are still moving — in fact, you might be moving fast — but you are not doing anything. The slope is carrying you. That is coasting.

When a vehicle moves forward under its own momentum, without being powered, it is coasting.

  • You stop pedaling on a bike, but it keeps rolling forward. → You are coasting.
  • A car runs out of fuel on a gentle slope and glides forward silently. → It is coasting.
  • A sled reaches the flat ground at the bottom of a hill and slides onward. → It is coasting.

The key detail: the movement isn't powered by current effort. It is carried by momentum (energy built up before) or gravity (the slope doing the work). The moment you start pedaling or hit the accelerator, you are no longer coasting — you are actively driving.
The Figurative Meaning (About People and Situations)

This is the more common, everyday use of the word. When a person coasts, they are getting by without trying their hardest, usually relying on something already in place — their talent, an easy environment, or past achievements — rather than putting in real work.

  • "He coasted through school." → He passed without really studying. Things came easily to him and he never pushed himself.
  • "She has been coasting on her early success." → She did something impressive years ago, and now she is living off that reputation instead of working hard.
  • "The team coasted to victory." → They won very comfortably, barely needing to try, because they had built such a big lead.
  • "He is just coasting at work." → He is doing the minimum needed to keep his job, not growing, not striving.

In all of these, the person is moving forward — passing school, keeping a job, winning a game — but the real engine is not current effort. It is either an easy situation or something from the past.

It depends on the situation.

In physical contexts, coasting is completely neutral. There is nothing wrong with a bicycle rolling downhill. It is just a description of what is happening.

In human contexts, coasting usually carries a mildly negative tone — a quiet suggestion that someone could be doing more but is not. It implies a kind of comfortable laziness, an absence of ambition or drive. When someone says "he's just coasting," they are almost always expressing mild concern or disappointment.

That said, it is not always a criticism. "They coasted to the championship" can sound admiring — it means they won so easily it looked effortless. Context matters. The negativity tends to appear when effort was expected but withheld.
The One Idea That Ties It All Together

Whether physical or figurative, the word always carries this single truth:

Progress is happening, but no active effort is powering it right now. Something from before — or something external — is carrying things forward.

You are along for the ride.

• Coast along — to continue at a comfortable, easy pace without challenging yourself.

"He's been coasting along for years with no real goals."

  • Coast on (something) — to use a past achievement or natural advantage as a substitute for current effort.

"You can't coast on your reputation forever."

  • Coast to a stop — (physical) when something gradually loses momentum and stops on its own, without braking.

"The ball rolled across the floor and coasted to a stop near the wall."

  • Coast to victory/the finish — to win or complete something with ease, without being seriously challenged.

"With a 30-point lead, they coasted to the finish."

The beauty of this word is its elegance. It captures — in a single syllable — the exact feeling of gliding forward on borrowed energy, feet off the pedals, wind in your face, doing nothing at all.
